title: 2  Overview of Quantitative Methods
text:
2.1 Main designs in quantitative research
Quantitative research in applied linguistics is characterized by the systematic investigation of phenomena that can be represented, at least in part, in numerical form. We then use these numbers to do fancy statistics to test hypotheses. In essence, we are using our domain expertise in the language sciences to make guesses about some topic of interest—say, speech perception in early bilinguals—and then quantify our uncertainty around the answer we obtain. Unfortunately, this process is not trivial. A good quantitative study includes numerous core elements that require a considerable investment of time, resources, and careful, deliberate consideration. In this chapter, we consider some of these investments of time. For instance, a robust quantitative study will likely include, but is certainly not limited to, the following: a clearly articulated research question or hypothesis, an explicit theoretical framework, operational definitions of constructs, a defined population and sampling strategy, procedures for data collection, an analytic plan, and a framework for statistical inferences. All of these core elements are associated with explicit training and careful planning in successful quantitative research.
At the heart of this approach is the notion that the phenomenon under investigation—be it speech perception in bilinguals, processing speed, instructional effectiveness, or any other number of interesting topics—can be meaningfully quantified. Researchers must therefore justify not only the choice of measurement instruments, but also the argument that the numerical indicators they collect validly represent the underlying construct. This process of construct operationalization is not merely technical; it is theoretical. Decisions about how to measure “proficiency”, “input”, or “interaction” embody assumptions about what those constructs are and how they manifest in observable behavior.
We are only two paragraphs in and this may already feel a bit overwhelming, depending on your level of experience with quantitative research in linguistics. Don’t fret. In this chapter we overview the key elements of a quantitative study with the goal of bringing you up to speed, or refreshing your memory, regarding what we see as the critical topics. Let us continue by pointing out that the mere process of observing linguistic behavior is inherently complex. At its core, observation is the use of the senses for some motivated purpose. Much to our chagrin, our senses are not always reliable and may not necessarily present an accurate representation of reality. Why is this so? Well, to simplify, first we have a sensation of some sort, and then we make use of evolved adaptive mechanisms (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste) to decipher the sensory input. In other words, our perception is a reconstruction of a sensation into a meaningful message in the brain, which we must reinterpret so that we can make sense of it. The fact that sensations must first pass through our perceptions to be interpreted creates a neurological game of telephone that, to some degree, separates us from reality. How far that separation is from reality really depends on how one observes data. For some researchers, impressionistic data is the norm. For others, specialized equipment may handle the heavy lifting of observation, as is often the case with behavioral, neural, or physiological data.
So where does the quantitative part of a quantitative study come from? Where are all the numbers? After the complicated process of observation, we can begin to consider measurement, which we will operationalize as the process of assigning a number to an observation. In most experimental research this step is unavoidable, every observation must somehow be turned into a number, and these numbers are (hopefully) not arbitrary. In some cases, measurement can be quite simple, like counting the occurrences of some linguistic event (e.g., code switches, or the use of a variable form). In other cases, measurement can require sophisticated equipment to monitor physiological behavior (e.g., pupil dilation during reading) and specialized software to ascribe a value to the observation. In both cases, measurement involves a meaningful, defined process that requires both reliability and replicability for it to be valid. We will have more to say regarding replication in Chapters X and Y, but, for now, let’s briefly consider study design.
The logic of study design in quantitative research generally follows a straightforward sequence: question, design, data collection, and analysis. Although this sequence sounds simple enough, each step constrains the others in meaningful ways. The type of question a researcher asks largely determines the type of study that should be conducted. For example, a question about causal effects may call for an experimental or quasi-experimental design, whereas a question about relationships among variables may be better addressed with a correlational or observational approach. Linguistic research is typically more observational in nature (Grieve 2021). From this point further decisions continue to have downstream consequences. For instance, the design of the study can constrain the kinds of statistical analyses that can reasonably be applied to the data. Not every statistical model is appropriate for every research design, and careful alignment among research questions, study design, and analytic strategy is essential for producing meaningful, interpretable results. We will revisit this issue in Chapter X.
Another key component of study design involves identifying the population of interest and extracting from it a sample that is meaningful and representative (more on this below). In applied linguistics, the population might consist of early bilinguals, heritage speakers, classroom learners, or some other group defined by linguistic, social, or educational characteristics. It is rarely possible to observe every individual in a population, which is why we build statistical models, i.e., to generalize some finding of interest to the larger population. One notable exception may occur in studies involving speakers of an endangered language, where, in some cases, it may be feasible to observe the entire population. In such cases, sophisticated statistical modeling may not be necessary because the purpose of the research may not require generalization. For this reason, researchers must rely on samples. However, sampling decisions, like who or what is included, how participants are recruited, or how large the sample is, to name merely a few, have important consequences for the conclusions that can be drawn. If, for example, the sample is not representative of the broader population, the findings likely will not generalize beyond the particular participants who took part in the study. Focusing on the big picture, transparent reporting of sampling procedures and inclusion criteria is imperative for a study design to be robust and reproducible.
A critical distinction that often shapes quantitative inquiry is the difference between confirmatory and exploratory research. In confirmatory investigations, researchers begin with hypotheses derived from theory and test them using an analytic approach specified a priori, often with a preregistration or in a registered report. The key component here is theory. Exploratory research, by contrast, often involves searching for patterns in the data that may generate new hypotheses or reveal previously unnoticed relationships. This type of research is much more common in areas of inquiry that might be more novel and not yet have robust theory to pull from. Importantly, both approaches are valid and play crucial roles in the development of knowledge. At the same time, they differ in the strength of the conclusions that can be drawn and in their susceptibility to what are sometimes called researcher degrees of freedom (Gelman and Loken 2014; Simmons et al. 2011). This phrase refers to the many small analytic decisions researchers can make after seeing the data—for instance, how variables are coded, which observations are included, or which statistical model is ultimately reported. These decision points are sometimes described as “forking paths”, because each choice can lead the analysis in a slightly different direction. Whereas confirmatory research aims to reduce researcher degrees of freedom as much as possible, exploratory research takes advantage of them! In short, the two approaches serve different purposes.
Closely related to this discussion is the distinction between research questions and hypotheses. Research questions tend to be broad and descriptive, outlining the general phenomenon under investigation. Hypotheses, on the other hand, are specific and testable predictions about how variables should relate to one another. You may have noticed that some studies you read tend to have one or the other, and some may even have both. Being explicit about whether a study is exploratory or confirmatory—and about which decisions were made before versus after examining the data—may clarify whether your study includes general research questions or specific hypotheses. A good study makes these decisions and distinctions explicit, which, in turn, helps readers interpret the strength of the evidence being presented. It also contributes to greater transparency and reproducibility, both of which should be considered central goals of contemporary quantitative research in applied linguistics.
Having outlined the general logic of quantitative research, we now turn to the question of what kinds of study designs are actually used in practice. At a broad level, most quantitative research in applied linguistics can be grouped into three general categories: experimental, quasi-experimental, and observational designs. In experimental research, the defining features are control and random assignment. Researchers manipulate one or more variables and randomly assign participants to conditions, which sets the stage for making claims about causality. Quasi-experimental designs share many similarities but lack full random assignment, which is often difficult (or impossible) to achieve in real-world educational or social contexts. Observational designs, by contrast, involve measuring variables as they naturally occur, without manipulation. Much of applied linguistics research falls into this latter category, where the goal is often to identify patterns and relationships rather than to establish definitive causal links. Each of these approaches has its strengths and limitations, and, as we have already suggested, the choice among them should be driven by the research question at hand rather than by convenience or habit.
Another important distinction concerns how data are structured over time. Many studies in applied linguistics are cross-sectional, meaning that data are collected at a single point in time, often comparing different groups (e.g., beginner vs. advanced learners). These are typically between-participant designs, where different individuals contribute data to different conditions. In contrast, longitudinal designs follow the same participants over multiple time points, allowing researchers to track development, change, or learning as it unfolds (Nagle 2023; Ortega and Iberri-Shea 2005). These are often within-participant designs, where each participant serves, in some sense, as their own point of comparison. In a similar vein, we can also make a distinction between real-time and apparent-time approaches. Real-time studies observe change directly, often over months or years, whereas apparent-time studies infer change by comparing groups assumed to represent different stages (e.g., age groups or proficiency levels). As you might imagine, longitudinal, real-time research can be resource-intensive (Ortega and Iberri-Shea 2005), but it provides a level of insight into developmental processes that cross-sectional designs simply cannot offer.
Beyond these more traditional designs, applied linguistics has also seen substantial growth in corpus-based research and classroom-based intervention studies. Corpus-based designs rely on large collections of naturally occurring language data, which can be analyzed quantitatively to identify patterns of usage, variation, or change. These studies often involve decisions about corpus composition, annotation, and representativeness that parallel, in many ways, the sampling issues discussed earlier. Classroom-based and educational intervention studies, on the other hand, are typically concerned with evaluating the effects of instructional practices or pedagogical innovations. These studies frequently operate under real-world constraints—limited control over participants, variability in instructional contexts—that make them prime candidates for quasi-experimental or mixed designs. In both cases, careful attention to design, measurement, and analytic strategy remains essential for producing credible findings.
Finally, it is worth noting that not all quantitative research fits neatly into a single design category. Mixed-methods approaches, for instance, combine a quantitative core with qualitative data (e.g., interviews, observations, learner reflections) to provide a more comprehensive account of the phenomenon under investigation. Similarly, replication studies and multisite research projects are becoming increasingly important in the context of reproducibility. Replication involves repeating a study—sometimes as closely as possible, sometimes with deliberate modifications—to assess the robustness of its findings. Multisite studies extend this logic by collecting comparable data across different contexts, populations, or research teams (REFS AND EXAMPLES). Both approaches help address concerns about generalizability and reliability, reminding us that a single study, no matter how well designed, is rarely the final word on any given research question.

text:
2.2 Main data analysis procedures in quantitative research
We now turn to what many readers associate most directly with quantitative research: data analysis. This is the stage where all of the prior decisions about research questions, design, sampling, and measurement come together. Importantly, data analysis is not simply a matter of “running statistics”, but rather involves aligning the structure of the data with an appropriate analytic framework so that the results meaningfully address the original research question. One of the first considerations in this process is the structure of the data itself. In applied linguistics, data are often nested (e.g., students within classrooms, responses within individuals), longitudinal (collected over time), or involve repeated measures (multiple observations per participant). These structures pose important challenges for conducting sound data analysis. To provide just one example, consider the standard linear model, which, historically, is the primary analytic tool used across disciplines for statistical inference. A key assumption of the linear model is that observations are independent, i.e., one observation should not provide information about subsequent observations. Importantly, failing to satisfy this assumption (and others) can result in a misspecified model and potentially misleading conclusions. In short, how your data are organized should directly inform how they are analyzed.
Before any complex modeling takes place, however, researchers typically begin with descriptive statistics. These include measures of point estimates, such as means or medians, as well as a measure of spread, like a range or standard deviation. At this stage, it is also important to consider data visualizations, like histograms or boxplots, to help understand point estimates and measures of spread. Although sometimes treated as a preliminary or even perfunctory step, descriptive statistics play a crucial role in understanding the data. They allow researchers to identify patterns, detect anomalies, and assess whether the data behave in ways that are consistent with expectations. In some cases, descriptive statistics may be indicative of an upstream issue with the data collection procedures or could even provide meaningful insights; in others, they serve as a necessary foundation for more advanced analyses. Either way, careful attention to descriptive statistics helps ensure that subsequent inferences are grounded in a clear understanding of the data at hand.
Closely tied to both data structure and description are decisions about measurement and scoring. Recall that quantitative research depends on assigning numbers to observations. How those numbers are derived is not always straightforward. Researchers must decide how to score responses, how to handle missing data, and how to aggregate or transform variables. In many cases, especially when working with tests, questionnaires, or rating scales, these decisions are informed by psychometric considerations such as reliability and validity. For example, do multiple items intended to measure the same construct actually correlate? Do scores remain stable across iterations of the task? These are not trivial concerns. Poor measurement can undermine even the most sophisticated analysis, whereas well-constructed instruments provide a solid foundation for meaningful inference.
When it comes to modeling relationships among variables, many analytic approaches in quantitative research can be understood within a broader regression framework. Put simply, regression involves estimating the relationship between one or more predictor variables and an outcome variable. This general logic underlies a wide range of techniques, from simple linear regression to more complex models used for categorical or non-linear outcomes. Thinking in terms of regression provides a unifying perspective: regardless of the specific technique, researchers are typically asking how changes in one set of variables are associated with changes in another. This perspective can help demystify what might otherwise appear to be a bewildering array of statistical methods.
Building on this foundation, more advanced approaches have been developed to handle the kinds of complex data structures commonly encountered in applied linguistics. Multilevel (or hierarchical) models, for instance, are designed to account for nested data, such as students within classrooms or repeated observations within individuals. Rather than ignoring this structure, these models explicitly incorporate it, allowing researchers to partition variability at different levels and obtain more accurate estimates. Similarly, structural equation modeling (SEM) provides a framework for analyzing relationships among latent constructs—variables that are not directly observed but are inferred from multiple indicators (e.g., motivation, proficiency). SEM allows researchers to model both the measurement component (how well the indicators reflect the construct) and the structural component (how constructs relate to one another), offering a powerful, albeit complex, analytic tool.
Finally, it is worth briefly addressing two broad statistical paradigms that underpin much of quantitative analysis: frequentist and Bayesian approaches. Without going too far into the technical details, frequentist methods—still the most commonly used in applied linguistics—rely on long-run frequency properties of estimators and often involve null hypothesis significance testing. Bayesian approaches, by contrast, incorporate prior information and update beliefs about parameters in light of the observed data. Each framework has its own assumptions, advantages, and limitations, and both can be used to address similar research questions. What is most important, from our perspective, is not strict allegiance to one paradigm over the other, but rather a clear understanding of the assumptions being made and a transparent account of how analytic decisions were reached. As with all aspects of quantitative research, thoughtful alignment between questions, data, and analytic approach remains the guiding principle.

title: 2  Overview of Quantitative Methods
text:
2.3 Methodological rigor in quantitative research

2.3.1 Participant Selection
One of the most fundamental aspects of quantitative research involves defining the population of interest and sampling from that population. In our view, populations are often defined too broadly, which can have downstream consequences for the scope of generalizability of the research. Consider, for instance, researchers working with university students who are learning an additional language in an instructed setting. In this case, it is easy to imagine that findings might generalize broadly, from one sample of university language learners to another learning the same language, or perhaps even a different one, depending on the breadth of the research questions asked and tasks used. Yet, this broad characterization of the population, which could lead to an equally broad application of findings, obscures many ways in which samples might differ. For one, the sociodemographic characteristics of the samples might be quite different if one is drawn from an elite private university versus a large, public, land-grant institution. Another possible difference could be geographic. Depending on where the universities are located, the language learning affordances of that region—the extent to which the target language is spoken outside of the classroom context, and therefore opportunities for language use and interaction—could vary considerably. Furthermore, the reality is that most researchers have historically relied on convenience samples, which means that samples could be affected by self-selection bias and thus may not be representative of the average language learner. In short, researchers must take care to define the population in precise terms and to take a critical approach to sampling by adopting strategies that mitigate the risk of sampling bias. How can this be accomplished?
In terms of defining the population carefully, two strategies are needed. First, the population must be described so that sampling can proceed in reference to a set of target characteristics. Second, sufficient information must be collected on the sample so that the description of the sample is as accurate as possible. This ensures that when future research on the topic is conducted and compared to the original research, differences in sample characteristics can be rigorously assessed. Typically, researchers have collected and reported on what we view as minimally adequate linguistic information related, for example, to participants’ language learning and use profiles. Yet, we see that information as important but limited in several ways. Regardless of study focus, sociodemographic information should be collected and reported. Sugden and Moulsen observed that “even if [a researcher is] not interested in the impact of race, culture, and ethnicity on the phenomenon under study, including these variables can add depth to researchers’ understanding of a phenomenon” (2015, 2). We concur and further argue that the collection of such variables is necessary for describing the sample completely and accurately. More comprehensive reporting can reveal systematic gaps in sampling, which can provide important information on the extent to which applied linguistics samples are overly WEIRD (Henrich et al. 2010) and academic (Andringa and Godfroid 2020). More purposeful sampling can also allow for interesting comparisons between randomly drawn (likely convenient) samples and more representative ones (Andringa and Godfroid 2020). Another consideration is to collect additional linguistic or socioaffective information that could be important for understanding the sample. For instance, in second language acquisition research, scholars have called for more consistent implementation of independent proficiency measures (Park et al. 2025). Such measures are necessary for providing more accurate proficiency information on the sample. Similar arguments could be extended to other variables, such as language learning motivation, with the goal of describing the motivational profile of participants included in the sample even if motivation is not central to the research questions. As another example, in applied linguistics research on bilingual samples, the primary construct of interest might be language dominance. Yet, it could also be useful to collect data on participants’ code-switching practices using a tailored questionnaire for that purpose (Olson 2024). Code-switching behaviors could affect the target phenomenon, but even if they do not, describing the code-switching characteristics of the sample could be an important data point for sample comparison in future work. Certainly, we do not advocate for adding more and more instruments to the research design to the point that it becomes unwieldy for the researcher and overly time-consuming for participants. However, we do encourage researchers to think about moving beyond minimally (in)adequate descriptions of the sample by considering what additional information about the sample might be necessary.
Sampling can be divided into two broad categories: probability and non-probability. Probability sampling is by definition random, in which case no subgroup should be over or underrepresented, provided the sample is large enough. Conversely, non-probability sampling involves a non-random process. This non-random process can be intentional or not. The convenience and snowball sampling that have been the bread and butter of our field are not intentional because via those techniques the researcher simply recruits as many people as possible, without attending to sampling bias. However, non-probability sampling can also be purposive, insofar as the researcher can define, a priori, what sample characteristics are desired and align sampling with those characteristics. In research on the incidence of non-native speakers showing nativelike ability, Andringa and Godfroid (2020) recruited native speakers of Dutch based on level of education and age. He also took care to recruit at several locations around Amsterdam, including educational institutes, supermarkets, and community centers, to capture a range of individuals. He was then able to construct representative and non-representative native speaker samples, while also noting that even the representative sample was not truly representative considering the demographic norms of the Netherlands because the lowest educational levels were not represented and the sample was not randomly drawn. Purposive sampling such as this is also used when researchers are interested in ensuring sufficient coverage on continuous target variables such as proficiency (Huensch and Nagle 2023) or aptitude. Put another way, if the researcher aims to assess the relationship between an aptitude measure and an outcome, then they must ensure that the sample shows a range of aptitude scores along the aptitude continuum and that the distribution of scores is approximately normal.
Up to this point, we have considered how to define and construct the sample in relation to the population, but we have not discussed how to actually recruit the sample, which is equally important and affects sampling quality. As @Sugden and Moulson (2015) pointed out, recruitment is an often overlooked aspect of sampling. In their study, they tested and compared different recruitment strategies to see which strategy would prove most effective. Strategy affects not just the sample that is ultimately recruited, but also the speed with which the target sample size is reached.
An enduring consideration for sampling is sample size, which is directly related to statistical power, or the likelihood of detecting a target effect. If the effect size is known or can be approximated, then sample size simulations can reveal how many participants are needed to detect the effect at 80% power, or 80% likelihood of detecting the effect if it truly exists. In general, the recommendation has been to adequately power studies, that is, to include the exact number of participants needed. Underpowered studies should be avoided because if the effect is not detected it may simply be due to power, and overpowered studies should be avoided because they are not efficient in terms of resources. Yet, sample size planning extends beyond simply powering a study to detect an effect, such as the standardized difference between a treatment and a control group. Indeed, researchers have also advocated for a consideration of sample size in relation to the width of confidence intervals, with the goal of estimating a narrower and therefore more precise interval for the target effects (Norouzian et al. 2018). It also bears mentioning that sampling and sample size planning does not just involve participants. Participants respond to items, and their speech may be evaluated by listeners, which makes items and listeners other populations of interest where sampling and sample size planning take on renewed importance. Furthermore, contemporary research also involves clustering, such as students within classes, or participants within sites, adding yet another layer to the sampling discussion. Historically, most of our research has focused on asking questions at the lower levels of data structure, focusing on participants, items, and listeners rather than on classes or sites, but as research moves forward, more complex simulations will be needed to compute power and determine sample size across all levels of data structure. [something on multi-level models here, if only briefly]
Options for recruiting participants have diversified in the digital age. In-person recruitment at the research site continues to be the primary means of sampling, but many researchers now recruit online, using platforms such as Amazon Mechanical Turk or Prolific or through social media and bespoke websites to promote citizen science. By going online, researchers can often reach much larger participant pools that they would not otherwise have had access to, and because of that fact, they may be able to recruit larger and more representative samples. Yet, the same sampling procedures and system of checks and balances that applies to in-person sampling also applies online. Namely, a population of interest must be defined, and once participants are sampled, the relationship between the sample and the population must be evaluated and convincingly established. Platforms such as Amazon Mechanical Turk and Prolific offer a variety of built-in filtering options that allow researchers to drill down to the specific population of interest, and researchers can also build and implement customized, study-specific filters. However, in online recruitment, participant attrition tends to be more pronounced, especially for studies requiring more than one session, which means that self-selection biases could be magnified in online samples. [something on reliability of online data collection, or save it for another section]


2.3.2 Data Collection Procedures
A fundamental aspect of data collection is developing valid and reliable instruments. Unfortunately, in many cases, validity and reliability are assumed rather than rigorously assessed and reported on. Sometimes, this information may get trimmed from a manuscript, or moved to an appendix or supplementary material, but the reality is that validity and reliability are not psychometric decoration but rather essential to the interpretation and generalizability of our work. Validity refers to whether the tasks we design actually measure what we intend to measure, and reliability refers to measurement precision. A survey or a questionnaire might be valid but not reliable. Likewise, a particular instrument might measure a phenomenon or construct precisely, but it may not be valid if the construct being measured is not the intended one. Traditionally, validity and reliability have been extensively discussed in relation to latent construct measurement. For example, if a researcher wants to examine motivation using a questionnaire, then they need to define what motivation is and develop items to measure it. Those items must be tied to their definition (validity) and they should tap into the same underlying construct and demonstrate internal consistency (reliability). In other words, they should pattern together. Importantly, even with high-profile models and measures, such as the L2 Motivational Self System, each time a questionnaire is used, validity and reliability must be established rather than assumed. In fact, doing so is part of the productive struggle and growth trajectory of a research domain. In L2 motivation research, the L2 Motivational Self System has come under scrutiny due to apparent jingle-jangle fallacies. That is, the term jingle, applies when the same name is used for different constructs, and jangle when different names are used for the same construct (see Al-Hoorie et al. 2024). Research adopting that framework has also been critiqued for assuming rather than assessing and demonstrating the reliability of motivational subscales (McClelland and Larson-Hall 2025). Certainly, the debate around this model is a sign of the complexity of the conceptual space and of disciplinary growth [ ] (Nagle, 2025), but the reality is that validity and reliability issues cannot be ignored, assumed, or moved to the margins of our research.
As another example, in speech research, speakers are recorded responding to a prompt, narrating a story using a series of images, or completing a standardized speaking test. A short stretch of speech is then extracted for presentation to listeners, who might be asked to transcribe it to quantify intelligibility or rate it using a Likert scale to quantify comprehensibility and accentedness. Several validity and reliability issues arise in listener-based evaluations such as these. For one, is one, 30-second excerpt representative of the speaker? Put another way, can we claim that the intelligibility, comprehensibility, and accentedness of the excerpt is representative of the speaker, or is it simply representative of that particular stretch of speech? To generalize from an excerpt to a speaker, and to examine the extent to which excerpts sampled from the same speaker pattern together and are evaluated similarly, multiple excerpts are likely needed (Crowther & Isbell, 2023).  Turning to the listeners, do they interpret and apply the rating scales consistently? For instance, if one listener rates sample A as more comprehensible than sample B (i.e., assigns a higher rating to A than B), then do the other listeners show the same pattern (A > B)? Rating scales and testing also bring to the forefront another issue: item or step discrimination. When an interval or ordinal scale is used, there is an assumption that the steps on that scale reflect discrete and higher levels of the property being rated. In interval scales, steps are also assumed to be equidistant. These properties can be tested to determine if scales are of an appropriate length, if the steps are clearly discriminable (i.e., if there is a true difference between, for instance, a rating of 5 and a rating of 6 on a 9-point scale), and so on, which is useful both on psychometric (How well is the scale performing?) and conceptual (How many levels of comprehensibility are truly identifiable in the data? Can participants be sorted into bands based on those levels?) grounds (Yamashita, 2026).  The same logic can apply to any test that is developed. A key aspect of test design is ensuring a range of item difficulty, such that items can separate test takers based on their ability. Some items are hypothesized to be harder than others and therefore useful for separating test takers at the higher end of the ability continuum, whereas others are easier and thus useful at the lower end. A test where all items are of relatively equal difficulty would not be very useful because it would lump together all participants or, at least, show poor separation of test takers at certain ability levels. (references to Isbell’s work)
An important challenge researchers face is how and where to document research procedures. Research presentations and publications are typically product-oriented, insofar as they describe the end-state of the research, that is, the finalized tasks and procedures the researcher decided to implement, without much space allocated to the actual process that led the researcher to make those decisions. Yet, this perspective is at odds with contemporary open science research practices, which emphasize discoverability, accessibility, reusability, and transparency. Certainly, researchers provide justifications for the decisions they have made, but those decisions are not often compared and contrasted with alternative paths, of which there are many. To put a point on this issue, when Coretta et al. (2023) assessed research degrees of freedom in the acoustic coding and statistical analysis of the same speech data set, they found that the 46 teams who participated produced 2,860 combinations. Had the teams entered the study at the data collection stage, the number of combinations would have been exponentially more. As the authors and other scholars (e.g., Bolibaugh et al., 2022) have pointed out, variation in research practices is not due to negligence, a lack of expertise, or some other factor, but rather a fact of life in a complex human-subjects discipline such as ours. This means that full documentation is more necessary than ever because without it, as the field moves forward in that area (e.g., via replication), it will be impossible to locate the source of divergent findings, which could be due to variables the research has systematically altered or an undocumented or underreported deviation in study design and implementation.
Whenever possible, we recommend that researchers (1) make their actual tasks, coding schemes, and procedures publicly available, (2) provide a log or another form of documentation describing changes, both intentional and unintentional, that took place during data collection, and (3) describe in detail any steps that were taken prior to data collection to validate instruments and other aspects of study design. (look at publicly available standards for this, other research articles that have described this)


2.3.3 Data Analysis Procedures
Data can often be coded and analyzed in a variety of ways. For example, if a test is administered to participants, the researcher may decide to compute a mean score and use that as the dependent measure of learning. Alternatively, they might decide to model the item-level response data. These two choices would lead to different statistical analyses, and as these decisions proliferate throughout the data coding and analysis pipeline, they will likely have downstream effects on results and interpretation. To illustrate this point, Coretta et al. (2023) invited teams of researchers to use a set of recordings that the lead authors had collected to answer a predetermined research question. Each team was responsible for determining, documenting, and reporting on their analytical choices, including the acoustic measures they decided to extract and how they did so, the models they fit, and any data screening and normalization procedures applied during the process. Quality checks carried out by the teams on one another’s analyses suggested that individual approaches were well motivated and documented. At the same time, there was a high amount of researcher degrees of freedom, and these degrees of freedom in decision-making had a real impact on each team’s results. Among other findings, the acoustic measure analyzed and the window over which it was analyzed had a notable effect on whether the target difference was observed and the magnitude of the estimate. This study, and others like it, underscores that the seeming objectivity of data analysis is at best a mischaracterization, if not an illusion altogether, because ultimately, even at this stage, the researcher must make complex decisions about what to measure, how to code the target variables, and what models to fit.
At the time of writing, mixed-effects modeling is the current standard for data analysis, usually within a frequentist framework (as opposed to a Bayesian approach), owing to the fact that most applied linguistics data involves some amount of clustering or hierarchical organization. In the open scholarship world, where multisite (or multiteam) analyses are becoming more common, participants are clustered within sites, or analyses within teams, and these links must be explicitly modeled to account for non-independent observations. Put another way, participants who take a test at one site are more likely to resemble one another—their data are more likely to be correlated—than they are to resemble participants at other sites. The same logic applies to multiple observations of the same individual, such as in a longitudinal study, where each participant contributes more than one observation, or in a multitask study, where each participant completes several versions of a task under different conditions. In fact, all studies involving more than one observation necessarily involve clustering. In a study where a participant takes a test consisting of 20 questions, the questions are nested in the participant, and in a study where a participant records ten words, the recordings are similarly nested or clustered. The latter is a hallmark of speech research where, for example, my pronunciations of a particular target feature are much more likely to show strong correlations with one another than with the pronunciations recorded by another person.
Mixed-effects models can be fit to data showing many different distributions, making them a flexible analytic choice. They are also robust in the face of missing data, and their assumptions tend to be more flexible. Because mixed-effects modeling is a regression-based analysis, assumptions on residuals (normality, homoscedasticity, and linearity) apply. The most powerful aspect of this technique, however, lies in the ability to model and estimate random effects, which quantify variance in the relevant parameter. Given an emphasis on individual differences in our field, random effects can be an appropriate way to ask and answer questions related to variability in learning and the variables that shape it, though at present, random effect structures are not always well specified, nor are they well utilized for hypothesis testing.
Entire volumes and many articles have been dedicated to this technique, so our goal is not to review this analytical approach extensively here. Instead, we briefly point out some of the major concepts behind it while also directing readers to relevant resources for further reading. First, fixed and random effects. Fixed effects are variables that we have observed as researchers (e.g., age of onset, language dominance, aptitude) or ones that we have experimentally manipulated (e.g., treatment condition). These variables are the typical independent variables included in all research, and they are considered fixed because their levels are stable, that is, they can be listed and their interpretation is straightforward from one study to the next. Random effects imply that units have been sampled from a larger population of possible units. Thus, they are non-exhaustive, and their interpretation is likely to change from one study to the next. Examples of random effects include participants, stimuli (words, images, etc.), sites, and so on. Random effect groupings can include intercepts and slopes. Intercepts represent deviation from the mean fixed effect for the target grouping. For instance, when random intercepts are fit for participants, an estimate is produced for each participant in the data set indicating how much that individual’s performance deviates from the fixed effect. Random effect estimates can therefore be negative, indicating that the unit is below the mean level, represented by the fixed effect, or positive, indicating that the unit is above that level. Random intercepts can be conceived of as unit-specific deviation from the mean. Some participants will perform better and some worse, and likewise, some items will be easier or harder to respond to. Random intercepts are designed to quantify such intuitions. Random slopes can also be fit. Multiple regression implies generating a set of fit lines between predictors and outcomes to quantify how much the outcome changes as the predictor changes. Deviation in that relationship can be estimated via random slopes. For example, in a study on change over time, the relationship between time and the outcome is estimated. The fixed effect represents the average developmental trajectory, or the average amount that the outcome can be expected to change over time. Yet, some individuals will learn better than others, and some items might show greater improvement than others. By-participant and by-item random slopes for time can capture these nuances. As this brief overview shows, fitting such models demands complex decision-making related to building and testing the model and dealing with the inevitable convergence (the model could not reach a stable form) and singularity (one or more of the variance components in the random effects could not be reliably estimated) issues that will arise. Furthermore, statistical significance testing is not straightforward when using these models because p values are approximated, creating yet another decision point for scholars who must determine how effects and models will be evaluated: by approximating a p value or by comparing nested models to one another. In the case of the latter, what models get built and compared, and how those comparisons are carried out has been an area of sustained debate that spans both conceptual (Should a model be formulated based on a combination of theory and the specific hypotheses to be tested?) and mathematical (Should a model be formulated to account for potential interdependencies in the data?) domains.
Sensitivity analyses can help mitigate the knock-on effects that these decisions can have on results and subsequent interpretation. This procedure hinges on adopting several plausible approaches at relevant decision-making junctures, with the goal of determining the extent to which the various approaches produce similar findings. The goal is not to guarantee convergence, but rather to gain insight into how analytical choices affect outcomes, which in turn provides a more comprehensive portrait of the stable effects that persist across choices versus those that are highly dependent on the decisions made. The ultimate manifestation of this approach is a multiverse analysis, where a much larger number of analytical paths are pursued. Ultimately, this too involves researcher judgment regarding how to set the analysis up (how many and which alternatives to pursue, at which stages of the data analysis process, etc.).
It is easy to see how the complex decision-making involved at the data analysis stage can lead even the most well-intentioned researchers to engage in questionable research practices (QRPs), which range from lack of transparency in reporting data coding, cleaning, and analysis to p-hacking and hypothesizing after results are known (HARKing). Forty percent of researchers surveyed in Isbell et al. (2022) reported deleting data based on a gut feeling, as opposed to clear exclusion criteria. Likewise, 40% also indicated that they chose a statistical analysis based on a favorable outcome. When taken at face value, such decisions could be interpreted as negligent or even fraudulent behavior, but as Bolibaugh et al. observed, “the lifecycle of any research study is beset by a series of decisions, many of which are essentially arbitrary, whose consequences are usually unknown” (2022, p. 804). Set against this backdrop, open scholarship practices have great potential to shine a light on the oft hidden layer of decisions that shape research findings, allowing researchers to question, critique, and improve upon the science in future work, such as by reanalyzing available data using an alternative approach or collecting new data altogether. Over time, this contributes to a more transparent, reliable, and credible body of evidence on the topic. Certainly, as Isbell et al. (2022) recommended, researcher training with respect to critical issues (p-hacking, HARKing, and other QRPs) should be improved, but even experienced researchers make mistakes or engage in practices that are standard at the time but later may be replaced by more appropriate and sophisticated techniques. Creating a transparent record of exactly what was done, how, and why is therefore essential. Preregistering studies and analysis plans are the most robust check on questionable research practices. They serve the dual purpose of creating an opportunity for researchers to reflect on the design and envision what an appropriate analytical approach might be once the data are collected. The preregistration also functions as guide rails once data analysis is ready to begin, insofar as they are a straightforward blueprint for how to proceed. Crucially, such plans do not preclude additional analyses beyond what was preregistered. Rather, preregistered analyses are identified as “planned” and new analyses as “exploratory,” further solidifying a transparent record of the data procedures guiding the research.

title: 2  Overview of Quantitative Methods
text:
2.4 Reporting Practices
If we accept that research decisions are somewhat idiosyncratic and that no two researchers will converge on the exact same design and analysis plan (Coretta et al. 2023) (Bolibaugh et al., 2022; Coretta et al., 2023), then transparent and comprehensive reporting becomes our most important tool for understanding and advancing the state of the art. Yet, figuring out what to report is not necessarily an easy task given the complexities of human-subjects research. Rather than providing an exhaustive list, here we comment on a few areas that are routinely underreported or misunderstood in terms of their reporting. We also point to resources that are now available, including templates that provide a reporting roadmap. First and foremost, validity and reliability underlie everything we do, but researchers often leave out critical information on both topics. Regarding validity, a case must be made that the instruments actually measure what we intend to measure and, in fact, are the most appropriate instrument because usually there are many different options available, each of which may be appropriate for a particular population, research context, and so on. Related, when surveys and tests are administered, reliability must be established upon each administration rather than assumed. The fact that a survey showed good reliability in previous research does not mean that it will prove reliable in the current study. At the time of writing, there was some controversy regarding the validity and reliability of the constructs included in individual differences research on motivation, notably the L2 Motivational Self System. Briefly stated, as the field has expanded, more and more individual difference measures have entered the research space. Beyond the specific context of the L2 Motivational Self System, researchers were critiquing a set of larger issues that are relevant to all research: imprecision in terminology (jingle-jangle fallacies), which can exacerbate measurement issues and hamper the development of the field, and lack of reliability checking and reporting, among other more targeted issues. Intra- or intercoder/rater reliability must be similarly checked and reported using an appropriate approach. Thus, validity and reliability apply throughout the research process, from instrument development to coding decisions.
The field has focused intensively on statistical significance within the null hypothesis significance testing (NHST) framework, leading to an overprioritization of p values. This, in turn, has created several reporting problems for the field. First, researchers may not report and discuss nonsignificant results in manuscripts, or they may shelve the manuscript altogether. Nearly 50% of researchers indicated that they had engaged in one of these two forms of omission in Isbell et al.’s (2022) survey. Second, p-values may not be appropriately contextualized. An effect may be statistically significant, but its effect size, or practical significance, must also be interpreted. To be clear, effects should not be judged as interesting or not based on their size. Indeed, many effects in the social and behavioral sciences are likely to be in the small to moderate range, yet those effects may be especially important or interesting. Effect size must not be reified in the same way that p-values should not be. Rather, they must be interpreted alongside a host of other important statistical information, including confidence or credible intervals, which provide a range of plausible values that could be compatible with the data and therefore encode uncertainty.
Modeling decisions are also underreported, especially with respect to random effects, where researchers may not provide a rationale for selecting a particular random effects structure and/or may not interpret the random effects when discussing results. We have seen two common approaches: adopting a minimal random effects structure, consisting of only random intercepts while ignoring potentially informative and necessary random slopes, and adopting a maximal structure, where all possible random effects are fit (and subsequently often pruned due to convergence and singularity problems). Neither is particularly desirable because, just as fixed effects should be aligned with the research design and represent the hypotheses that the researcher aims to test, so too should random effects. Put another way, the random effects structure should reflect the beliefs the researcher has about the data, that is, beliefs about where variance is likely to be observed. Though uncommon, random effects can also be mapped onto variance-based research questions.
These issues are embedded in a constellation of reporting decisions that researchers must make. The sheer amount of reporting required, and where it should take place—in the main manuscript, in appendices or supplementary materials, as part of an open scholarship package linked to the manuscript but not explicitly discussed in the submission—is daunting. Yet, many useful resources exist for this purpose. The guiding principle for reporting should be reproducibility: Could a researcher take the current information and, reproducing the design decisions from start to finish, arrive at the same result on the same data? Could a researcher replicate the study completely collecting data from a new sample of participants? Templates such as the OSF preregistration template and the Language Learning submission requirements for Registered Reports. There are also training materials such as Wood et al.’s (2024) volume on Addressing Questionable Research Practices in Applied Linguistics, and targeted tutorials on a variety of methodological topics, including many related to statistical modeling and several on open research practices such as computational reproducibility (In’nami et al., 2022).
No matter how much we report, all research has its limitations. One way of addressing limitations explicitly and from a positive perspective is through a constraint on generality statement, which invites the researcher to reflect upon the populations, contexts, tasks and so on to which the results are likely to apply, as well as those that fall outside of the scope of the current study. These statements are useful for researchers and practitioners alike. For researchers, it establishes a potential roadmap for future replication work. For practitioners, it can promote a better understanding of when findings are likely to apply, which can be especially helpful for determining whether an intervention is likely to work well for a practitioner’s learner population and in their teaching and learning context.

title: 2  Overview of Quantitative Methods
text:
2.5 Critical quantitative research
A common misconception is that the stance to share data is just that: a stance. Nonetheless, once one has made the decision to share, the work has just begun, as many issues suddenly become important. For instance, one has to consider where they will share their data, how exactly they will share it, and they have to go through the process of documenting the data so that it is usable. All of this implies a great deal of work that requires specific workflows, all of which must be given careful consideration and should not be taken for granted. To make the issue even more complex, it is also important that this whole process is traceable with a research path. That is to say, the workflow must be reproducible to both the original author and future users. Learning how to do all of the above is not straightforward and represents legitimate barriers to entry that can cause fear and anxiety for researchers.

2.5.1 What is data? Data vs data set
An additional fear has to do with the notion of getting scooped. Many researchers believe that once they have collected data, it would be counterproductive to then make it publicly available, presumably because somebody else could use it to produce a research product that the original author intended to produce before they actually did it. This is often referred to as being ‘scooped’. In our experience, scooping is uncommon. Nonetheless, the fear of being scooped seems to be persistent in academia. Unfortunately, when a data set is shared publicly, one cannot guarantee that somebody else will not use the data in a way the original author intended (before they are able to do so). We believe this fear is irrational for several reasons. First, given what we know about researcher degrees of freedom in linguistics (See Coretta et al. 2023), we believe it would be highly unlikely for two (or more) independent research teams to approach a future analysis in exactly the same way. Thus, any resulting research products would necessarily be different from each other in non-trivial ways. Second, we believe it is important for researchers to distinguish between raw data and the data sets that are derived from them, e.g., audio recordings in wav format (raw data) vs. a csv file with formant frequency values (derived data set). Researchers typically make derived data sets available to the public. Future research from the same project often involves deriving a new data set from the raw data, e.g., a new csv file of VOT measurements in milliseconds from the stop consonants in the raw audio files. The raw data vs. derived data set distinction is likely a reason why being scooped is uncommon and, in our view, an irrational academic fear. In addition, one could also view the use of public data by outside research teams as a potential opportunity to foster collaboration by inviting outsiders to participate in future related projects. Finally, despite all of the reasons given for which one need not fear being scooped, researchers still have the option to pre-register future studies. In other words, they can generate a time-stamped document in an open repository, such as the OSF, in which the implied use of all raw data to derive novel data sets—along with all corresponding hypotheses—is memorialized in time.
We have all heard uncle Ben’s advice to Peter Parker that with great power comes great responsibility (DELETE THIS). This also seems to ring true with regard to data analysis. One particular aspect of conducting quantitative research that is often overlooked, by both researchers and the general public, deals with what exactly we are quantifying for our analyses and whether or not this quantification is always the best, most ethical choice. Is it the case that research in some areas does more harm than help? Consider, for example, the long history of eugenics in the field of statistics. Many of the key procedures used to this day, across a plethora of fields, were developed out of the desire to push an agenda that would be deemed unacceptable in today’s world (I HOPE!). There are myriad examples in which it is conceivable that outside, nefarious motivation to ‘prove’ certain ideas could result in disfavorable outcomes for vulnerable communities. In the world of linguistics, this could be research conducted with indigenous languages, or research conducted on language learning with implications for pedagogy, or it could be research conducted on bilingualism with implications for public policy. Consider, for example, ‘English Only’ policies rampant in the US Southwest. The greater point that we want to make is that research always contains bias. The simple fact that a researcher is interested in a given topic shows bias in some way. Every choice that we make is influenced by some factors that we are conscious of and others that we are not. Many people are aware of this fact, but most do not consider how bias is also present in quantification. Sometimes it manifests in how we frame the quantifications that we make. For example, one may use slower reaction times as an indication of a negative performance in some task and then use this information to push a deficit view when comparing some population to another. For these reasons it is always imperative that we consider what we quantify, how we quantify it, and how we characterize those quantifications. We must strive to be as transparent as possible with the how and why when we quantify things, so as to bring to the forefront all of the conscious and unconscious biases our quantifications may represent.
There is no doubt that applied linguistics research (and, indeed, social science research at large) has focused on understanding language in Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD; Henrich et al., 2010) societies. Many of us work in WEIRD contexts, which means we sample WEIRD participants with the goal of generalizing to other WEIRD participants. Thus, this practice is not in-and-of-itself problematic. It becomes problematic when findings based on WEIRD participant samples and research practices are taken to be representative of the way language works at large, including outside of the WEIRD bubble. Many other forms of bias persist in applied linguistics research. We tend to focus on academic populations, and those findings may not (often do not) generalize to samples recruited outside of academic circles (Godfroid & Andringa, 2023). Participants often trend younger, owing to the fact that many of us work in a university context and therefore rely on convenience samples of college-aged learners, which means that we have captured language behavior during participants’ cognitive prime. This means that findings may not generalize to older (and younger) populations, whose cognitive profiles, hearing and vision, and so on may be quite different from those of college-aged adults. When results are positioned as definitive, we run the risk of constructing a normative model to which everyone else gets compared. Put another way, we may end up inadvertently reinforcing a modal view of language, where most individuals are assumed to follow a common path when in reality language and language learning are far more complex and variable than such a modal view would have us believe (see, e.g., Kutlu & Hayes-Harb, 2023; McMurray et al., 2023). [Something on neurodivergent learners; Kormos’ work?]
Another common area of sampling bias is language itself. Specifically, whose language practices get measured and how? Much applied linguistics work has focused on English. Again, this is not necessarily problematic because many researchers study the acquisition, learning, and use of English as a first, second, or additional language and therefore seek to generalize findings to that population. But, as above, when findings for English are overgeneralized and assumed to be representative of the acquisition, learning, and use of other languages, then we no longer have a field of applied linguistics but applied English linguistics.
These two issues go hand in hand, insofar as the language behaviors of certain groups may be positioned as the point of reference. One clear example is the trend of comparing bilingual and multilingual users, such as second and Heritage language learners, to (presumably) monolingual native speakers, creating a false dichotomy between native and non-native language users. This comes with the expectation that the goal is to somehow perform like a native speaker, which in turn can lead to a deficit view of language learning and use given that the linguistic experience and behavior of bilinguals will never fully match that of monolinguals. Furthermore, in an increasingly globalized world, where more and more individuals are learning additional languages through a combination of methods (e.g., informal language learning via apps like Duolingo, formal classroom instruction, immersion), the idea of a monolingual versus multilingual divide is increasingly blurry. The fact of the matter is that most, if not all, individuals at some point in their lives will engage in some form of language learning, and even in the off chance that they do not, with globalized media, it is likely that they will be exposed to a wider range of native and non-native varieties. They may even be exposed to additional languages. The rise of Korean language and culture through K-pop and K-dramas in recent years is one prominent example.
This reminds us of the dynamism of language and behavior and of applied linguistics as a field. Findings collected two or three decades ago—findings that many of us continue to reference in our work—may no longer be representative because, to put it succinctly, the world has changed, and language has changed with it. This, coupled with the fact that individuals have more language learning options than ever, means that language as a whole and individual practices are continuously evolving. This begs the question: When we measure language learning in a particular sample, or even in a particular individual, how do we account for the dynamics of this process? How much do we need to measure to stand a chance of providing at least a semi-accurate snapshot of the linguistic systems of the individual user, who may speak multiple languages comfortably, dabble in others via apps and global media, and so on? This issue is not trivial because when we design our studies, we are faced with the task of developing a small battery of tasks that can render an image of a complex, dynamic system.
If a tree falls in the forest but nobody hears it, does it make a sound? If applied research is published but few can read it, does it make an impact? Research is typically paywalled, so if someone wants to access it, they have to pay a fee. The irony is that researchers themselves—the very individuals who have produced the work—can find themselves locked out of their own research. A typical research-to-publication timeline looks like this. First, the researcher does the work, writes it up, and submits it to a journal. Then, the journal editors, most of whom are faculty and researchers themselves, solicit external reviews, and these reviews also come from other researchers. Once the review process has played out, if the decision is made to accept the research for publication, it moves to copyediting, typesetting, and then “printing,” except that most publications are almost exclusively accessed online, so no printing is required. Once the article is in this final stage, the authors can choose to make the article open access by paying a fee. This fee can be thousands of dollars. If not, the article is paywalled. An individual can access it by buying a copy, or an institution such as a university library can grant access to it by subscribing to the journal or a suite of journals all published by the same publishing house, such as Elsevier. This subscription can run tens of thousands of dollars a year, which creates an access problem because only wealthy institutions can afford such fees. In the most extreme case, then, researchers have produced the work, served as scientific editors, copyeditors, and reviewers for it, and at the end of the process, may find themselves unable to access it. The case for practitioners who may be interested in applying the research is far worse given that they probably do not have access to university libraries to circumvent paywalls. In short, our research often does not reach our target audience, and one major reason is related to financial access and the publishing industry.
This problem is not new, and researchers in our field have been working to address it for the past decade. First, a small, but growing, number of individual journals have either been created under an open access model (e.g., Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching) or have gone open access (e.g., Laboratory Phonology), ensuring that researchers and practitioners around the globe can actually read the research. Likewise, some publishing houses are also converting to open access publishing. Cambridge University Press, the publisher of Applied Psycholinguistics, Studies in Second Language Acquisition, and several other journals in our field, is a notable example. We expect that in the coming years, many other publishers will opt into this model, and if they do not, individual journals will stop renewing contracts and convert to open access on their own. Second, authors can now choose to publish a one-page summary of the research in plain language through the Open Accessible Summaries In Language Studies (OASIS) project (Marsden et al., 2018; see https://www.oasis-database.org/). These summaries are openly accessible regardless of whether the article is, and many journals (e.g., Foreign Language Annals, the journal of the American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Languages or ACTFL) now encourage researchers to publish them. A third means of getting the research to the public is through the post-print pledge (see, e.g., Al-Hoorie & Hiver, 2023). Journals prohibit sharing the final (copyedited and typeset) version of the manuscript, but many allow authors to share the accepted but pre-copyedited (Word) version widely. Currently, Ali Al-Hoorie maintains a website where authors can look up journal-specific information on what is sharable. Other tools such as the Open Policy Finder (https://openpolicyfinder.jisc.ac.uk/) can also be used for the same purpose.
The goal underlying all these initiatives is singular: to ensure that scholars and practitioners can actually read, use, and build upon the work we are doing, which is essential for advancing applied linguistics as a field. Importantly, they also create a more equitable and just research space. If research is open, then all researchers, regardless of context and institutional support, have the opportunity to participate in our scientific and scholarly community. Likewise, practitioners can access the work and put findings into practice, and at its best, this research-practice-appraisal cycle can inform future work, which can in turn generate more robust and (practically) meaningful evidence.
This raises another important point: Who is research actually for? And, relatedly, does our research model enable meaningful participation by all stakeholders? A quantitative view of research inevitably lends itself to treating participants as bundles of numbers, or objects of quantification. Certainly, part of quantitative methods is determining how to capture a complex, dynamic phenomenon like language numerically in a way that is valid, reliable, and reproducible. At the same time, we have to remember that the numbers are not the people, and we also have to ask ourselves how we can make the numbers work for the people that get included in the research. In other words, as researchers, we should be concerned about returning the data—either literally, in terms of making the data available, or metaphorically, in terms of ensuring that the findings based on the data are made known to and used for the benefit of—our participants. Currently, our field encourages open science through open science products, such as open materials and procedures and open data and analysis code. As mentioned, there is also a strong emphasis on making the research products (publications) open and accessible. Yet, once those products are out there, do they matter? Is making things available all we are called to do as open scientists? Put another way, should there not be some translational aspect of actually returning the data and findings to the very participants we collected it from? This does not mean data validation and checking, or asking participants to review study components for accuracy. Rather, it means ensuring that our findings are applied to benefit the very people who set aside time to provide the data in the first place, often with the understanding that findings will make things better for them and for similar individuals in the future.
Open science is often regarded as the new frontier for research, and in our experience early career researchers typically want to (or feel compelled to) participate in open science initiatives but may not know how. This is indicative of a bigger problem related to how we as individuals and as a field can systematically support training and onboarding into open science practices in ways that do not contribute to academic burnout and othering. [More on this]
We work in a pressurized academic environment where productivity is king, funding is scarce, and time is at a premium. All these factors can work against open science, which by its very nature requires us to slow down, plan carefully, and document everything not just in a way that makes our work transparent and legible to us but also to others. It’s not surprising that scholars may approach open practices with skepticism and even dismay. After all, many of us already feel that our plates are full, so the prospect of adding another component to our research can generate anxiety. We understand and share these feelings. Early-career researchers may feel overwhelmed by the open science landscape. Even if they recognize the importance of engaging in open science, the demands of the publish-or-perish model may lead them to forgo open science before tenure. For more established scholars, the models they grew accustomed to using during their early career may persist. The reality is that the further along we get in our careers, the less time and energy we have for the learning required for new research activities such as an emphasis on open science. We have also noticed a trend for scholars to regard open science as an all-or-nothing endeavor. We reject this view for several reasons. First, nobody becomes an expert overnight. Expertise comes with time, training, and frankly the mistakes we make as we learn and improve. Second, applied linguistics as a field has recently reached the critical mass of open scholarship practices to enable the next step in our collective open science journey: developing open science training materials that are scaffolded, sustainable, and freely accessible. This book represents one such material, but many others are already available or soon to be so.
Thus, rather than viewing open science as something to be achieved, we invite readers to reflect on openness as something to approach. As we move through our careers, learn new skills, and find new research interests, what open science means and what our open science practices look like will necessarily change. We believe our emphasis should be not just on transparency—that is, on documenting what we have done—but also on our own reflexivity as researchers, which amounts to reflecting on the “why” behind it all. The “what” and the “why” go hand in hand because decisions can be arbitrary or intentional. When the “why” is not made clear, the “what” can be taken as gospel, leading future researchers to replicate design decisions that may have been well informed for a specific context but would not work in another. Likewise, researchers may reproduce design choices that were essentially arbitrary because as several scholars have pointed out, researchers make hundreds of decisions based on many factors. A dual emphasis on transparency and reflexivity allows us to approach our work with epistemic humility.
